briefs.headline: India draws record $127 billion through forex deposits: RBI
briefs.bodyText:
India mobilised a record $127.23 billion through foreign-currency deposits under a special central bank programme aimed at strengthening the country’s foreign-exchange liquidity, highlighting the role of the overseas Indian community in supporting the economy during periods of market stress, the Reserve Bank of India said on Wednesday.
Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank), or FCNR(B), deposits accounted for $127.226 billion in inflows as of August 31, the RBI said.
Including overseas foreign-currency borrowings (OFCB) and external commercial borrowings (ECB), total inflows under the measures stood at $136.377 billion.
The strong response prompted the RBI to close the FCNR(B) window a month ahead of schedule. The facility, launched on June 8, was originally scheduled to remain open until September 30 but was closed on August 31 after the central bank said its objective had been achieved ahead of schedule.
FCNR(B) deposits are fixed-term deposits held in foreign currencies, with the principal and interest repaid in the same currency. This allows non-resident Indians to park foreign-currency funds with Indian banks without taking direct exposure to rupee exchange-rate fluctuations.
The inflows give Indian banks and the RBI a larger pool of foreign currency to manage external pressures and support liquidity in the foreign-exchange market, particularly during periods of heightened rupee volatility.
The RBI did not provide bank-wise mobilisation figures. However, private-sector lender ICICI Bank said separately that it had mobilised $17.88 billion through FCNR(B) deposits up to August 31.
Loans provided by the bank’s international branches and subsidiaries against such deposits stood at $9 billion, while standby letters of credit issued to other banks against loans backed by the deposits amounted to $3.63 billion.
The RBI measures included absorbing hedging costs for banks mobilising FCNR(B) deposits and allowing banks to lend against the funds. The initiative was aimed at strengthening India’s external-sector position and improving foreign-exchange liquidity amid global uncertainty.
Overseas foreign-currency borrowings contributed another $5.26 billion, while external commercial borrowings brought in $3.891 billion, according to provisional RBI data.
The latest mobilisation is reminiscent of India’s response to the 2013 “taper tantrum”, when the RBI introduced a special FCNR(B) swap scheme to attract foreign-currency deposits from overseas Indians as the rupee came under severe pressure following the US Federal Reserve’s plans to reduce its monetary stimulus.
The 2013 scheme mobilised around $26 billion in nearly three months and was followed by a sharp recovery in the rupee. Foreign-currency assets received through the latest swaps will be reflected as foreign-currency assets on the RBI’s balance sheet, potentially adding to the country’s foreign-exchange reserves.
India’s forex reserves rose by $12.422 billion to a record $729.328 billion in the week ended August 21, according to the latest RBI data.
The finance ministry said last week that the large-scale mobilisation of long-term non-resident deposits and institutional funding would strengthen India’s external buffers while providing foreign-currency resources to banks and companies, news agency PTI reported.
It also said the response reflected the continuing role of the Indian diaspora in supporting India’s financial and economic growth and confidence in the resilience of the Indian economy and banking system.
The record inflows came as India’s economy showed resilience despite heightened global uncertainty. GDP grew 7.8% in the April-June quarter, beating expectations and the RBI’s 7% forecast for the period.

stories.headline: US Open Third Round: Sabalenka crushes Iatcenko 6-1, 6-1; rain delays pile up
stories.deck: Aryna Sabalenka stormed into the US Open third round with a 6-1, 6-1 win over Polina Iatcenko in just 53 minutes. Jessica Pegula also advanced quickly, while rain caused major delays across New York. Despite disrupted schedules, Alex de Minaur, Ben Shelton, Daniil Medvedev and Karolina Muchova progressed. The first round was finally completed Wednesday night.
stories.bodyText:
Aryna Sabalenka made a huge statement at the US Open, cruising into the third round with a dominant 6-1, 6-1 win over Polina Iatcenko in just 53 minutes.
The world No. 1 looked sharp and powerful after arriving in New York under pressure following a string of early exits.
Sabalenka was nearly flawless on her first serve, winning 15 of 16 points in the opening set and 21 of 28 overall. She is aiming to become the first woman since Serena Williams from 2012-14 to win three straight US Open titles.
“Happy with the level I played today, happy with the focus and happy to be through this match,” she said.
Third seed Jessica Pegula also reached the third round quickly, defeating Sofia Kenin 6-3, 6-1 in 56 minutes.
“To be out of there in under an hour, it doesn’t always happen,” Pegula said. “So I think I’m just going to take that one and run, I guess, until the next round.”
Rain causes more delays
Rain continued to disrupt the tournament, with matches on outside courts repeatedly stopped while play under the roofs at Arthur Ashe Stadium and Louis Armstrong Stadium continued.
The weather also forced several players to wait days before completing their opening matches. 
Spain’s Paula Badosa eventually beat Daria Kasatkina 6-1, 6-4, while Australia’s Alex de Minaur finally began his campaign with a 6-2, 6-2, 6-4 win over Andrea Guerrieri.
“It’s been a couple tough days. But I mean, these tournaments, it's all about adapting and that’s the name of the game,” de Minaur said. “There’s too much to play for to let something like this affect you.”
The first round was finally completed Wednesday night, with 25 men’s singles matches played as organisers tried to recover from the delays. Several seeded players, including Ben Shelton, Daniil Medvedev and Karolina Muchova, also advanced.

stories.headline: Messi’s Argentina No.10 successor revealed as 21-year-old star awaits one condition
stories.deck: Nico Paz has reportedly been chosen to inherit Lionel Messi’s iconic No.10 shirt for Argentina, marking the start of a new era after Messi’s international retirement. The 21-year-old Como star would take over the legendary number if coach Lionel Scaloni renews his contract, with Argentina reportedly viewing Paz as a key figure for the future.
stories.bodyText:
Lionel Messi's retirement from international football has left Argentina with one of the most difficult shirts in world football to fill. The No.10 has belonged to Messi for years after previously carrying the legacy of Diego Maradona, and the player reportedly chosen to inherit it is one of Argentina's brightest young talents. Nico Paz has emerged as the reported successor to the iconic shirt, but there is one important condition attached to the plan.
Nico Paz reportedly chosen to inherit Messi's No.10
According to ESPN Argentina, Argentina have already identified Paz as the player they want to hand Messi's No.10 shirt to, although the decision is tied to Scaloni's future with the national team.
The 21-year-old attacking midfielder has previously worn No.18 during his 11 appearances for Argentina, but he could now take on the number associated with two of the country's greatest-ever footballers.
ESPN Argentina insider Federico Bueno reported that the plan has already been decided internally and is being taken seriously.
"If Scaloni renews as Argentina's coach, which is expected to be negotiated in the coming months, the No. 10 shirt will go to Nico Paz. This has already been decided internally and is being taken very seriously," Bueno said.
That means Paz's succession of Messi is not yet unconditional. Scaloni's contract situation must first be resolved, with the 48-year-old expected to negotiate a new deal in the coming months.
Scaloni has been Argentina's head coach since 2018 and oversaw the side's run to the 2022 World Cup title in Qatar before taking them to the 2026 World Cup final. If he agrees to continue in the role, Paz is reportedly set to become the next No.10.
Why Paz has emerged as the choice
There are more established names within the Argentina squad who could have been considered for such an iconic shirt, including Enzo Fernandez and Alexis Mac Allister, but the reported succession plan points towards Paz as the player viewed as capable of leading the next generation.
Paz, 21, was born in Spain but is the son of former Argentina international Pablo Paz. He came through the Real Madrid academy and made eight first-team appearances for the Spanish giants before leaving for Italian club Como in 2024.
His development in Serie A has accelerated under former Arsenal midfielder Cesc Fabregas, with Paz establishing himself as one of the most exciting young attacking players in European football.
He has made 77 appearances in all competitions for Como, scoring 19 goals, while his performances have repeatedly fuelled speculation that Real Madrid could bring him back to the Bernabeu.
A return to Madrid has reportedly been tipped in virtually every transfer window since his departure, underlining how highly the Spanish club continues to regard the player it developed.
For Argentina, however, his development has taken on a different significance.
Paz has already earned 11 senior caps and is now being considered for a role that carries considerably more weight than simply becoming another attacking option in the squad.
Messi leaves behind an enormous legacy
Whoever takes the No.10 will inevitably be compared with Messi, even if Argentina's next generation has no realistic way of reproducing what the eight-time Ballon d'Or winner achieved.
Messi departs the national team as a former world champion, having captained Argentina to glory in Qatar in 2022, and as the country's long-standing No.10 and leader.
He leaves after 207 international appearances, having built a legacy that also places him as the second-highest goalscorer in World Cup history.
Argentina's Lionel Messi (10) cries at the end of the World Cup final soccer match between Spain and Argentina in East Rutherford, N.J., near New York, Sunday, July 19, 2026. (AP Photo/Stephanie Scarbrough)
His decision came after Argentina's defeat to Spain in the 2026 World Cup final in New Jersey, with Messi making clear that he felt his international journey had reached its natural conclusion.
"It was a decision that hurt – and still hurts deep down – but I understand that the time has come," Messi said in his retirement statement.
"I swear to you that I always gave it my all – not just in these last few years when we won everything, but before that too; I always fought and left everything on the field for this jersey, to bring you joy and make you feel proud to be Argentine through football."
"Time is running short, chapters come to a close, and this is one that hurts me deeply. I love, have loved, and will always love being part of the national team."
"I’ve given everything I had; I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are some great young players coming up who deserve to be here."
A huge shirt for Argentina's next generation
The significance of the No.10 means Paz would not simply be inheriting a squad number.
Argentina's shirt has already carried the weight of Diego Maradona, who famously wore it during his World Cup-winning campaign in 1986, before Messi created his own extraordinary chapter in the number.
That makes the decision to give it to a 21-year-old a significant statement about how Argentina view Paz's potential.
The Como playmaker is still at an early stage of his international career, with only 11 appearances to his name, and he has never been expected to simply replace Messi as a player. Instead, the reported decision reflects the belief that he can become one of the central figures in Argentina's post-Messi era.
There is still one hurdle before that succession can happen.
Scaloni's future must first be settled. If the World Cup-winning coach agrees a new contract, the reported plan is for Paz to move from the No.18 he has worn during his early international career into Messi's iconic No.10.
For now, that remains a reported internal decision rather than an officially confirmed shirt change. But if Scaloni stays, Paz appears set to become the young Argentine entrusted with carrying the most famous number in the country's football history into its next era.

stories.headline: Federer’s final masterpiece: Roger’s homecoming to the Hall of Fame
stories.deck: Once a boy who broke racquets and scrubbed toilets for it, Federer turned a hot temper into quiet grace and routine brilliance into religion, becoming tennis’s closest thing to a spiritual experience. In Newport on Sunday, the Hall of Fame simply made it scripture.
stories.bodyText:
There should be a word for what Roger Federer did on a tennis court, because “played” barely covers it. Watching him felt like being granted a glimpse of the divine, and that’s no exaggeration. Your jaw went slack, your eyes bulged, and sounds escaped your body that no grown adult should make over a man hitting a felt ball with a string racquet.
Federer did not invent anything. Every shot in his arsenal had been struck before, by someone else in some other era. Yet, in his hands, the borrowed became the sacred, the familiar became revelation, as if the shot had been waiting its whole life for him specifically to unlock it.
And he didn’t do it once in some career-defining flash of magic. He did it for the better part of two decades. It was a residency in genius, not a hot streak. Pete Sampras once said Federer’s game had no weaknesses, and it stands true. What other players built entire careers on – a single jaw-dropping moment etched into a highlight reel – Federer treated as routine.
Except, of course, that routine came around roughly a thousand times, spread across four Grand Slams and every corner of the world, and it never once stopped feeling like the first time. That is the strange arithmetic of Federer’s greatness: repetition should have dulled the wonder, but it never did. Familiarity, in his case, only sharpened the awe.
ALSO READ | Decoding Eala Mania — the movement sweeping across tennis
Now the residency has its plaque. The felt ball has been put down, the sermons have ended, and what’s left is the reckoning every great career eventually meets – not a match, but a monument.
On Sunday, the world celebrated Federer once again as he was inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame. It is the sport’s great farewell and its eternal afterlife in the same breath, a place where a player’s brilliance is carved into permanence, even as it reminds them that greatness is never solitary.
The crowd said as much. Billie Jean King, Martina Navratilova, Stefan Edberg, John McEnroe, Andy Roddick and many others were on hand to celebrate one of tennis’s finest champions.
And closer still sat the ones who needed no introduction. His parents, Robert and Lynette. His wife, Mirka, and his four kids that the tennis world had watched grow up, one Slam at a time, in players’ boxes scattered across the globe.
Mirka spoke first and introduced her husband with a line that outshone every statistic that followed. “What makes me proudest isn’t what Roger accomplished when the world was watching. It’s who he is when nobody’s watching,” she said.
He, too, glowingly praised the one person who has seen the highs and lows of his stardom from a touch away, while also building a semblance of a normal life together.
“Mirka inspires me every day. She showed me how to stay focused on tennis and take joy in everything else. A wonderful mother to our four kids… she makes the impossible happen. We grab each other’s hands, and we run through walls.”
More than trophies
For once, the man who made the impossible look routine was undone by his own history. He tried, and failed, to hold it together – pausing a few times to wipe his eyes, half-laughing through his tears. At one point, he pleaded for tissues and sunglasses, but pressed on anyway, the way he always had.
When he steadied himself enough, he spoke not of the trophies or numerous records. He was more focused on the more than 5,000 headbands he wore, the more than 7,000 pairs of socks he went through, some 10,000 racquets strung over the years, and the thousands of sets played on the same two knees.
“I tried to show my love for the game. Because it really mattered to me, and I also wanted it to matter to you. To be worthy of your attention, worthy of your attendance, because people don’t have to come watch us play. They come to be entertained, inspired, excited. They could always decide to go somewhere else, but they chose tennis, they chose us,” he emphasised.
The 45-year-old even wandered back to where it all began, not in any packed stadium but in the shadows just off it.
“I remember being a ball boy in Basel, standing against the back wall, hands behind me, eyes on the ball. I’ll never forget how the game looked from there… the intensity, the adversity, the feeling of being so close to the players. I remember the next morning, my legs were gone… standing all day is a lot of work.”
ALSO READ | Alexander Zverev and the contours of tennis’ new ‘Big Three’
Federer, especially later in his career, had the power to make the smallest cog in the wheel seen and appreciated. His core memory helped him do the same once more at Newport.
“I really want to thank every ball kid who ever stood through my matches or all our matches, for that matter, for hours on end. I see you. I thank you. I was you.”
It’s a strange, fitting symmetry: that is precisely how everyone felt watching his career unfold. Standing still, eyes fixed on the ball, absorbing the intensity as though they were pressed against the back wall of the court – even from several hundred or several thousand kilometres away, on the other side of the television screen.
More than a hundred titles in his cabinet, and yet Federer insisted the number was never the point.
“They call this the Hall of Fame… but fame was never the goal. My goal was to spend my life doing something I love, with people who love it as much as I do.”
And he did – relentlessly, joyfully, for the better part of his life. Federer didn’t just win; he took tennis to altitudes it hadn’t reached before, wrote storylines the sport had never dared to script, and handed the world rivalries (with Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic) that will be studied and mythologised for generations.
Smashed racquet, softened man
There was a time when the future maestro was closer to a menace. As a boy in Basel, he didn’t play tennis so much as wage a war with it – swearing between points, smashing racquets and the whole kit and caboodle. At 16, he tore through a practice backdrop, understandably earning a week-long toilet-scrubbing sentence from his coach.
By his own admission, the unlearning took years and was no epiphany. The real turning point wasn’t a victory or defeat, but a tragedy – the death of his childhood coach Peter Carter in 2002, which recalibrated Federer for good.
Self-deprecation became an art form, just like most things would with Federer. The same man, on Sunday, would hold up two aging knees to a crowd of legends and grin, saying, “Still got them, by the way. If I fall, please catch me.”
The once hot-headed boy is now at ease with laughing at himself, and became the most graceful man in tennis – on the court and off it. And he did it all with the same unhurried smile, even in the moments when the headband was fighting a losing battle against the sweat of yet another title run, even when his body was being pushed past what bodies are supposed to give.
“I’m still writing my love letter to tennis. My time as a player is done, but tennis will always stand at the intersection of everything I care most about… my family, our friendships, the past 40 years and the future we’re building. So this is not a goodbye,” he stated.
“We all leave the court eventually, but the sport keeps evolving. This boy from Basel thanks you… and I thank all of you for sharing the journey.”
ALSO READ | Linda Noskova: the calm warrior with heavy artillery
It is the tennis world, though, that owes its thanks to Federer. He carried the sport to spaces it had never been invited into before – into living rooms of people who couldn’t tell a forehand from a backhand, into the vocabulary of art critics and poets who had never once written about sport, into a kind of beauty that made the utilitarian business of winning feel almost secondary. He turned rivalry into reverence, opponents into co-authors, and a simple racquet into something closer to a paintbrush.
The ball boy became the main event. And the boy who once stood against the back wall, eyes fixed on the ball with hands behind his back, has finally taken his place among the very heroes he once watched from the shadows.
That, perhaps, is the only ending fitting enough: not a farewell, but a homecoming.

stories.headline: Cricketers to get best rooms at Asian Games, says Japan chief
stories.deck: A Sri Lankan official said this week that some of Asia's top teams had raised doubts over facilities and accommodation at the Games, which are taking place in Nagoya and the wider Aichi area from September 19.
stories.bodyText:
Cricketers at this month's Asian Games in Japan will have better accommodation than athletes from many other sports, the head of Japanese cricket said on Wednesday (September 2, 2026), after concerns were raised about a lack of five-star hotels for players.
A Sri Lankan official said this week that some of Asia's top teams had raised doubts over facilities and accommodation at the Games, which are taking place in Nagoya and the wider Aichi area from September 19.
Cricket is a minor sport in Japan and games will be played at a new purpose-built ground with reports of tents serving as dressing rooms and distant washroom facilities.
There is no dedicated athletes' village at the Games, with organisers instead relying on cabins in a cruise ship, rooms in temporary wooden containers and hotels.
Organisers said last week that accommodation was already stretched to the limit after the number of Asian Games athletes ballooned to 17,000.
By comparison there were around 11,000 at the 2024 Paris Olympics.
The cricket tournament is being run by the Asian Games organising committee in collaboration with the Asian Cricket Council (ACC).
Naoki Alex Miyaji, the CEO of the Japan Cricket Association, told AFP that the two bodies had been discussing accommodation options "for a long time".
"The participating teams in cricket are being offered hotel accommodation," Miyaji said on Wednesday.
"Many other sports are being accommodated in much more limited facilities such as a cruise ship or container hotels."
Matches will be played at Korogi Sports Park, a converted baseball field that is a 40-minute train ride away from central Nagoya.
Media reports in India said the country's cricket board was unhappy with arrangements and might send a second-string squad after originally naming 15 players led by Shreyas Iyer and including 15-year-old rising star Vaibhav Sooryavanshi.
Miyaji said that Japanese organisers "only had 17 months to prepare and had to start from scratch" for cricket at the Games.
He said they had been working "to ensure that the best facilities are provided within the limited timeline and facility restrictions".
"Despite being temporary, the facilities will provide as comfortable a space as possible for the players and officials," he said.
Miyaji said the pitch, which is being prepared by the curator of the 35,000-capacity Pallekele International Cricket Stadium in Sri Lanka, would be of a high standard.
"From what I have seen, the playing surface and field will be the best seen in cricket's inclusion in the Asian Games," he added.

briefs.headline: Mbappé named in kidnap plot: 26 rich targets, gang allegedly run from jail cell
briefs.deck: French investigators reportedly found Kylian Mbappé’s address among information on 26 wealthy individuals discovered on phones seized from an 18-year-old suspect. The teenager allegedly continued running a criminal organisation from prison and was reportedly planning kidnappings. Authorities are investigating whether the alleged operation progressed beyond identifying potential targets, with the…
briefs.bodyText:
Kylian Mbappe
 was reportedly among 26 wealthy and high-profile individuals whose addresses and personal information were found by French investigators during an investigation into an alleged kidnapping plot. The Real Madrid and France star was said to have been one of several potential targets identified on mobile phones seized from an 18-year-old suspect who was allegedly continuing to run a criminal organisation from prison. The list reportedly also included a rapper, a Chinese businessman, jewellers and a Turkish meat trader.
Mbappe among 26 alleged targets
According to French newspaper Le Parisien, investigators discovered the addresses of 26 wealthy individuals on two mobile phones seized from the 18-year-old suspect, identified as Clément L.
Mbappe was reportedly among the names on the list, alongside a rapper and several wealthy businessmen. Those other alleged targets included a Chinese businessman, jewellers and a Turkish meat trader, with investigators reportedly finding information that could have been used to identify or locate them.
The discovery came as authorities investigated the activities of the teenager, who allegedly continued directing a criminal organisation despite being held in prison.
The case therefore concerns an alleged plot rather than a kidnapping that was carried out. Investigators are now seeking to determine how far the organisation had progressed, whether any of the potential targets were actually approached or monitored, and what each person under investigation allegedly did.
Mbappe's inclusion is nevertheless particularly striking given his status as one of the most recognisable footballers in the world and his position as Real Madrid and France's captain.
Suspect allegedly ran gang from his prison cell
Clément L was already in pre-trial detention in connection with allegations of pimping and organised robbery when investigators discovered that he was allegedly continuing to issue instructions from inside prison.
According to Le Parisien, prison guards seized two mobile phones from him. Investigators then examined their contents and reportedly found information relating to the 26 alleged targets.
The teenager was allegedly operating on Snapchat under the alias "Lester Z", using the phones to communicate and issue instructions to people outside the prison.
A source close to the case told Le Parisien that the contents of the phones were particularly revealing.
"Two phones were seized by prison guards, and their contents were highly revealing," the source said.
The same source added: "He also wanted to go after a rapper and the footballer Kylian Mbappe."
The investigation reportedly began after authorities were looking into a separate robbery at a luxury watch shop in Neuilly-sur-Seine last April.
Clément L had already been identified as one of two men allegedly involved in the attack on the watchmaker, which had led to his detention over armed robbery.
The discovery of the phones subsequently opened a much wider line of investigation into the alleged criminal organisation and its potential plans.
What happened when the teenager was questioned?
During questioning, Clément L reportedly rejected the suggestion that he was the mastermind behind the alleged operation.
He also asked to be released from solitary confinement, but that request was refused and he was ordered to remain there while the investigation continues.
The teenager reportedly dropped out of school during the first year of a vocational qualification in cooking. He told investigators that he wanted to resume his education and eventually become a chef.
Despite those claims about his future plans, he remains in pre-trial detention as authorities investigate the much more serious allegations surrounding the criminal organisation.
His alleged accomplice has meanwhile been released under judicial supervision. That individual was challenging the measure on Wednesday before the Versailles investigating chamber.
The investigation must now establish precisely how the alleged kidnapping operation was organised, how much preparation had taken place and whether the information found on the seized phones translated into concrete plans against any of the 26 people named.

briefs.headline: In 2010, a Wimbledon match got so long the scoreboard simply broke
briefs.deck: John Isner and Nicolas Mahut produced the longest match in tennis history at Wimbledon 2010, battling for 11 hours and five minutes across three days. Their deciding set lasted eight hours and 11 minutes, with Isner eventually winning 70-68. The marathon produced 183 games, 215 aces and a scoreboard-breaking scoreline, later inspiring HBO’s “7 Days in Hell.”
briefs.bodyText:
A tennis match that lasted 11 hours and five minutes, stretched across three days, produced 183 games, and eventually broke the electronic scoreboard sounds more like a story written for television than something that actually happened at Wimbledon. Yet that was precisely what unfolded when American John Isner and France's Nicolas Mahut met in the first round of the 2010 Championships. Their fifth set alone lasted eight hours and 11 minutes, longer than some entire professional matches, while both players repeatedly served to stay alive in a contest that seemed to have no natural ending. By the time Isner finally won 70-68, the match had become a record that remains untouched and a sporting absurdity that later inspired an HBO mockumentary.
The match that refused to end
Isner and Mahut began their first-round match on Court 18 at the All England Club on June 22, 2010, and neither could have known that they were about to spend three days playing one of the most extraordinary matches in tennis history.
The opening four sets were already a serious contest, with Isner taking the first 6-4 before Mahut levelled with a 6-3 set. Mahut then edged the third 7-6, only for Isner to take the fourth by the same scoreline and force a deciding set.
That was where the match became something entirely different.
With the final set requiring a player to win by two clear games, neither man could create the decisive break. They held serve again and again as the score climbed through the 20s, 30s and 40s, with the match already far beyond anything Wimbledon had seen before.
Play had originally been suspended because of fading natural light after the first four sets on June 22. The players returned the following day, but the fifth set still could not be completed, with darkness once again forcing the match to be stopped.
They came back for a third day on June 24, still locked together.
By then, even the electronic scoreboard had effectively conceded defeat. It stopped functioning at 47-47 in the fifth set because it had not been programmed to record a score that high.
70-68: the fifth set that became its own match
The numbers from the deciding set are difficult to comprehend even when written down.
The fifth set lasted eight hours and 11 minutes and contained 138 games, with the players producing an astonishing 215 aces across the entire match: Isner hit 112 and Mahut 103.
They also held serve for 168 consecutive games during the match, while Mahut had to serve to stay alive 63 times.
There were only three service breaks in the entire contest.
Eventually, after hours of holding serve, Isner finally won the 137th game of the fifth set to move ahead, before breaking Mahut in the following game to end the marathon at 70-68.
The complete score read 6-4, 3-6, 6-7, 7-6, 70-68, with the match lasting 665 minutes, or 11 hours and five minutes.
The final set alone was longer than the longest baseball game on record, which lasted eight hours and six minutes.
The 183 games played overall were also 71 more than the previous highest total at Wimbledon, while the 138 games in the fifth set were 26 more than had been played in any other match.
Isner and Mahut had also eclipsed the previous record for aces in a match, which had stood at 78, with their combined total of 215.
"I have never seen anything like it," Isner said afterwards, while the scale of what had happened was summed up by his prediction that "Nothing like this will ever happen again, ever."
Neither player was quite the same afterwards
The physical demands of the match became obvious immediately.
Isner returned to the court for his second-round match against Dutchman Thiemo de Bakker, but lost in straight sets, with the effects of the three-day battle clearly still hanging over him.
Mahut's defeat was equally extraordinary in its own way. Despite losing, he had produced one of the most remarkable individual performances in tennis history, with the two players setting records for points, games and aces that were unlikely to be approached again.
The appeal of the match was not simply the final score, however, because as the fifth set moved beyond 50-50, both players were visibly exhausted while continuing to produce the physical effort required to keep the contest alive. Mahut repeatedly chased balls at full stretch, while Isner was visibly struggling between points, yet neither could find the small lapse that would finally end the contest.
The fact that it was a first-round match on an outside court made the spectacle even stranger, with two players who were not among the sport's biggest global stars suddenly becoming the centre of attention as word spread about what was happening on Court 18.
The match was so extraordinary that Wimbledon later commemorated it with a plaque outside Court 18.
A plaque commemorating the Isner–Mahut match on Court 18 at Wimbledon/Wikipedia
Isner and Mahut met again in the first round at Wimbledon in 2011, but there was no repeat marathon, with Isner winning in straight sets.
The record changed tennis
The Isner-Mahut marathon was possible because of the Grand Slam rules in place at the time, which required the final set to continue until one player established a two-game advantage.
That system has since changed at the major tournaments, making another 70-68 deciding set increasingly difficult to imagine.
Wimbledon now uses a tie-break when the final set reaches 12-12, while the Australian Open uses a first-to-10-point super tie-break at 6-6. The French Open has also retained the advantage-set principle in its deciding sets.
Isner himself would later find himself at the centre of another Wimbledon marathon. In the 2018 semi-finals, he lost to South Africa's Kevin Anderson 7-6, 6-7, 7-6, 4-6, 24-26 after six hours and 36 minutes.
That match became the fourth-longest in tennis history and the second-longest at a Grand Slam, but the repeated marathon matches contributed to Wimbledon eventually introducing its fifth-set tie-break.
Other records remain well behind Isner and Mahut's mark. The longest Grand Slam final in the Open Era was the 2012 Australian Open final, where Novak Djokovic defeated Rafael Nadal 5-7, 6-4, 6-2, 6-7, 7-5 after five hours and 53 minutes.
The longest women's singles match lasted six hours and 31 minutes, with Vicki Nelson beating Jean Hepner 6-4, 7-6 at the 1984 Central Fidelity Banks International tournament.
The longest doubles match came at the 2013 Davis Cup, when Tomas Berdych and Lukas Rosol defeated Switzerland's Stanislas Wawrinka and Marco Chiudinelli 6-4, 5-7, 6-4, 6-7, 24-22 after seven hours and two minutes.
None came close to the 11-hour, three-day ordeal in south-west London.
From Wimbledon absurdity to HBO
The story eventually travelled well beyond tennis.
The 2010 marathon helped inspire HBO's "7 Days in Hell", a mockumentary starring Andy Samberg and Kit Harington about two fictional tennis players locked in an impossibly long Grand Slam match.
Samberg later recalled watching the real-life Isner-Mahut match with writer Murray Miller and joking that somebody should make a film about a tennis match that simply never ends.
That joke became the 2015 HBO film, which exaggerated the premise to comic extremes, but its starting point was very real: two players, three days, 11 hours and five minutes, 183 games and a fifth set that reached 70-68 before anyone could finally walk off Court 18.
More than 16 years later, the Isner-Mahut match remains the Guinness World Record holder for the longest professional tennis match ever played.

briefs.headline: Towhid Hridoy creates history with 350, breaks Tamim Iqbal’s long-standing record
briefs.deck: Towhid Hridoy has etched his name in cricket history with a breathtaking innings of 350 runs, becoming the first Bangladeshi player to achieve this feat in first-class cricket. He has surpassed Tamim Iqbal's former record of 334 runs while also setting the bar for the highest score by a foreign batter on South African soil. The match resulted in a draw, and South Africa A wrapped up the series…
briefs.bodyText:
Bangladesh A captain 
Towhid Hridoy
 etched his name into the country's first-class record books after becoming the first Bangladeshi batter to score 350 runs in an innings. The landmark knock came at the NWC Oval in Potchefstroom on Wednesday, more than six years after Hridoy helped Bangladesh win the Under-19 World Cup at the same venue in 2020.
Resuming the fourth day on 204, Hridoy carried his bat through the remainder of Bangladesh A's innings and finished unbeaten on 350 off 481 deliveries, hitting 27 fours and 10 sixes.
His innings helped Bangladesh A declare at 676 for eight, giving them a 164-run advantage after South Africa A had posted 512 in their first innings. South Africa A reached 18 without loss before the teams settled for a draw.
Hridoy breaks Tamim's record
Hridoy's marathon innings made him only the third Bangladeshi batter to reach a first-class triple century. More significantly, he went past 
Tamim Iqbal
's unbeaten 334 and Raqibul Hasan's unbeaten 313 to claim the highest first-class score by a Bangladeshi batter.
He also became the first Bangladeshi to register a first-class 300-plus score outside the country.
The 350 was equally significant from a South African perspective. Hridoy now owns the highest first-class score by an overseas batter in South Africa. Only one other batter has crossed the 350-run mark in a first-class innings in the country, Stephen Cook, who scored 390.
Reflecting on the innings, Hridoy said the performance had given him considerable confidence and made him believe he could produce a similar effort at international level.
“To be honest, this innings gave me a lot of confidence. After picking the Man of the Match trophy I was feeling that someday I will play an innings like this in the national team,” Hridoy said after the match.
Tamim congratulates Hridoy after record falls
Tamim Iqbal, whose 334 had stood as Bangladesh's highest first-class score, was quick to congratulate Hridoy after his record was surpassed. Tamim said scoring 350 runs in any first-class setting was an exceptional achievement, but doing so in South Africa made the feat even more remarkable.
He also welcomed the fact that his record had been broken, describing Hridoy's achievement as a sign of the progress being made by Bangladeshi cricket.
South Africa A nevertheless took the four-day series 1-0. The hosts had dominated the opening match in Pretoria, winning by an innings and 413 runs, before Hridoy's record-setting performance helped Bangladesh avoid defeat in the second game.
The two sides will now switch to the 50-over format, with a three-match one-day series beginning in Bloemfontein on September 6.

briefs.headline: Tamil Nadu Ranji pre-season camp from September 3
briefs.bodyText:
Tamil Nadu will begin its pre-season Ranji Trophy campaign from Thursday in the city. The selectors have picked a 30-member probables list for the camp, with nine other players — mostly fast bowlers — set to take part.
Following a disappointing Ranji Trophy campaign last year, in which the team finished sixth among eight teams in its group, TN desperately needs to pull up its socks this year.
For the fifth year in succession, TN will have a new coach in former player V. Yo Mahesh, who guided the State under-19 side to the semi-finals last year.
The camp will be spread across a couple of venues, including MAC Stadium, where it will also play a four-day game later this month.
Following the camp here, the team will travel to Ahmedabad to play a couple of pre-season games before heading to Jaipur for the opening Ranji Trophy fixture against Rajasthan, which starts on October 11.
Meanwhile, in a significant move, the association is set to appoint a new Head of Cricket in the next few weeks, who will be in charge of all the state’s teams. “He will be assisting the selectors and coaches and be involved in talent scouting and ensure the academy is run in the best way,” said TNCA President T.J. Srinivasa Raj.
“From this year, we plan to have monthly review meetings with team coaches, academy coaches and the Strength & Conditioning staff to keep a track on the progress of teams and players.”
“We are also in the process of reviving an old practice of having six to seven permanent coaches at the TNCA Academy. Apart from these permanent coaches, we will have a handful of coaches on short-term assignments who can assist during camps for the various teams,” he added.
For the camp, the curator has been asked to prepare some pitches with grass and bounce to help both batters and bowlers prepare for conditions they will get outside the State.
“We will also start earlier than usual around 8 a.m., so batters can play when there is a bit of moisture on the pitch. Though we can’t get identical conditions to what we will get up north, we will try our best to simulate it here,” said Srinivasa Raj.
Meanwhile, the MAC Stadium will host TN’s first home fixtures against Uttarakhand and Railways next month. This will be the first time Chepauk is hosting a Ranji game in two years, since the TN vs Karnataka clash in February 2024.

briefs.headline: Rohit’s future, ODI roadmap and recent setbacks on agenda at BCCI meeting
briefs.deck: Stalwart’s career, ODI team and the team’s poor performances in Ireland and England to be discussed as Indian cricket’s top brass meets on September 3 in Mumbai.
briefs.bodyText:
Mumbai/New Delhi:
 The future of Rohit Sharma and the shape of India’s ODI team for the next World Cup cycle are set to dominate discussions when the BCCI’s top brass meets in Mumbai on Thursday for a wide-ranging performance review.
While recent defeats in Ireland, England and Sri Lanka will be assessed, board officials are understood to be more concerned about the lack of a clearly defined ODI roadmap at a time when preparations for the 2027 World Cup should be taking shape.
BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia, president Mithun Manhas, head coach 
Gautam Gambhir
, chief selector 
Ajit Agarkar
 and Centre of Excellence chief VVS Laxman will attend the meeting, with ODI and Test captain 
Shubman Gill
 and T20I skipper Shreyas Iyer also expected to be present.
At the centre of the discussions lies the most sensitive issue facing Indian cricket: Rohit’s future. Though there is immense respect for the veteran opener’s stature and achievements, selectors and members of the team management are increasingly aware of the need to prepare for a post-Rohit era.
According to sources, one option under consideration is to evaluate Rohit’s role on a series-by-series basis rather than committing to a long-term plan through the entire World Cup cycle.
“It’s very tough on a young captain like Shubman Gill when there is no clear direction. The dressing-room environment in the ODI team hasn’t been the best, especially when it comes to dealing with stalwarts,” a BCCI source said.
The uncertainty around Rohit reflects a broader concern. Of India’s three national teams, the ODI side is regarded as the least settled. Injuries and workload management have prevented selectors from identifying a stable core, leaving several key positions unresolved.
The fast-bowling allrounder’s role remains a particular headache. Hardik Pandya continues on a managed workload programme after recurring fitness issues, while Nitish Kumar Reddy is yet to receive full clearance following rehabilitation.
“Hardik, at the moment, has been cleared to bowl six overs in a day. Reddy is still to clear his fitness tests. The ODI team doesn’t have even half of the core ODI team ready. It has to be a joint effort between the CoE and the team management to zero in on players and formulate a roadmap to get them all on the park as soon as possible,” the source said.
The review was initially planned after the Ireland and England tours but was postponed because of the subsequent Sri Lanka assignment. It will now cover India’s performances across multiple tours, including Zimbabwe and Sri Lanka.
India’s 2-0 T20I series defeat in Ireland and the 4-0 drubbing in England raised alarm bells, with the 125-run loss at Nottingham viewed internally as one of the team’s poorest performances in recent years. Gill’s ODI side also lost the England series 2-1.
However, officials insist the exercise will focus on solutions rather than assigning blame, with particular emphasis on recurring issues in preparation, selection and execution.
Fitness management is expected to be another major talking point. Jasprit Bumrah missed the Sri Lanka tour after aggravating a knee problem, while Washington Sundar, Nitish Kumar Reddy and Harshit Rana remain in line for fitness assessments at the Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru on Sept 9.
With a two-Test tour of New Zealand scheduled for Nov and a packed calendar ahead, the board wants tighter coordination between the medical staff, strength-and-conditioning team and national selectors to ensure greater player availability.
New role for Laxman
The meeting could also have significant administrative consequences. Laxman is being considered for an expanded role, with discussions continuing over a possible Director of Cricket position overseeing coaching, selection and player-development pathways. Agarkar’s tenure as chief selector, which ends later this month, will also come under review, with a one-year extension among the options being discussed.
Board President’s XI fixture vs visiting teams may be back
Meanwhile, BCCI is also examining the possibility of reviving the traditional Board President’s XI match before home series, following a recommendation from Manhas. The fixture, which historically featured leading domestic performers and Test hopefuls against visiting teams, has often served as a stepping stone for future India players while providing valuable match preparation to touring sides.

briefs.headline: Tilak says he wants to play in the Duleep Trophy final
briefs.bodyText:
South Zone skipper Tilak Varma expressed hope that he would be able to play the Duleep Trophy final against East Zone in Chennai starting this Sunday despite the short turnaround time between the marquee contest and the first T20I versus Afghanistan.
Tilak, who is India’s T20 vice-captain, will have to finish the final on September 10 and travel to Delhi for the international game scheduled for the 13th. East skipper Ishan Kishan and his deputy Vaibhav Sooryavanshi are also in the same boat.
“I want to play the final,” Tilak told reporters on Wednesday after the triumph over North Zone. “We have two days break in between. But it depends on the selectors and the management.”
Tilak hoped that speedster Vidwath Kaverappa, who didn’t take the field starting from the post-tea session on day three (Tuesday), will be available.
“His [left] ankle is slightly swollen, but he can walk and he is also running with a tape. I feel he will be there in the final. But let’s see.”
Karnataka stalwart Karun Nair, who scored 699 runs in the 2025-26 Ranji Trophy, was benched for the semifinal to accommodate Hyderabad’s K. Himateja. Tilak said it was purely because of team combination.
“North had two left-arm spinners, and we wanted a lefty in the middle-order. Himateja is a youngster (24) and has scored decent runs (485). It was very unfortunate for Karun.”

briefs.headline: Vishesh, Amardeep share halfway lead at Telangana Golconda Masters
briefs.bodyText:
Vishesh Sharma and Amardeep Malik sit atop the standings at 14-under 126 after the second round of the Telangana Golconda Masters here at the Hyderabad Golf Association on Wednesday.
Local favourite Vishesh (60-66), who matched the course record with an opening 10-under 60, followed it with a four-under 66 containing six birdies and two bogeys.
“The course played very differently compared with yesterday,” Vishesh said. “The fairways were much softer, the wind was considerably stronger, and the flags were tucked into more difficult areas. I had to adjust my strategy, aim for the correct sections of the greens and avoid chasing every flag,” the 19-year-old remarked.
Amardeep (61-65) made six birdies against a solitary bogey on the par-five 17th for a five-under 65. He later admitted that his opening score tempted him into playing more aggressively than the course demanded.
“I didn’t strike the ball particularly well today. There were stretches when I hit it nicely, but there were also moments when I left myself some challenging par saves. Fortunately, I managed to make the most of them, which is why I was actually happier with today’s round,” Amardeep said.
“After shooting a low number, the natural instinct is to attack again. But this isn’t a course you can overpower. You have to play intelligently, and I didn’t do that particularly well in a few places.”
Dhruv Sheoran (60-67) slipped one spot to third at 13-under 127. He mixed six birdies with a bogey on the par-five eighth and a double bogey on the par-four 18th, his final hole of the day, in a three-under 67.
Honey Baisoya (64-64) produced a second successive six-under 64, making seven birdies and one bogey to climb one place to fourth at 12-under 128. Bangladesh’s Md. Akbar Hossain (67-66) and Angad Cheema (66-67) shared fifth place at seven-under 133. Defending champion Jamal Hossain (72-66) of Bangladesh climbed from tied 72nd to tied 24th at two-under 138.
